title: Meet in Safe Places
body:
Meeting in a safe place is the first rule of secondhand buying because a private sale moves two strangers, cash or a device, and a valuable item into the same moment, and the place decides how much risk that moment carries. Safe places are public, staffed, well lit, and busy during the day: a police station exchange zone where one exists, a busy shop entrance, or a staffed public building. Unsafe places are the seller's or buyer's home, an empty car park at night, or any location the other party insists on after a safe alternative was offered. The insistence itself is information, and it should be treated as such.

Method. The working method for this record is a meeting-place score. First, list the proposed meeting's qualities: public, staffed, well lit, busy at the meeting time, and easy to leave. Second, mark each quality present or absent. Third, read the verdict: five qualities mean meet as planned, three or four mean meet only in daylight with someone told where you are going, and fewer mean propose a safe alternative or abandon the deal. Fourth, tell someone the meeting place and time, and take a charged phone. Fifth, the demo scores an example meeting place holding four qualities and prints the daylight-with-a-contact-told verdict.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for meet in safe places. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: safe qualities: 4 of 5; public: yes; staffed: NO; well lit: yes; busy at meeting time: yes; easy to leave: yes; verdict: daylight only, tell someone Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for every in-person secondhand exchange, without exception for small items, because small items still bring strangers together. Do not meet at a home address for a first transaction with a stranger, and do not let politeness override a bad location. Do not carry more cash than the agreed price, and do not let the meeting move at the last minute to a different, less public place. Do not use this record as a guarantee of safety, because a public place reduces risk rather than removing it. title: Inspect Before You Pay
body:
Inspecting before paying is the rule that makes secondhand buying work, because once money has moved, the buyer's leverage has moved with it. Inspection means handling the item, testing what can be tested, looking for the damage the photographs avoided, and comparing the item in hand with the listing's description line by line. A seller who rushes inspection, refuses a test, or demands payment before the item is examined is not protecting their time; they are preventing the buyer's only real check. The inspection should take as long as it takes, and the buyer should be willing to walk away from any item that fails it.

Method. The working method for this record is an inspection checklist scored before payment. First, list the inspection steps for the item: appearance against the listing photographs, function tested on the spot, damage and wear examined, included accessories counted, and serial or identifying marks noted where they exist. Second, mark each step done or skipped. Third, read the verdict: all steps done mean pay as agreed, one step skipped means complete it before paying, and more skipped mean do not pay yet. Fourth, note any difference from the listing in writing before paying, because a difference accepted silently becomes the buyer's problem. Fifth, the demo scores an example inspection completing four of five steps and names the missing step.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for inspect before you pay. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: inspection steps done: 4 of 5; appearance matches listing: done; function tested: done; damage and wear examined: SKIPPED; accessories counted: done; identifying marks noted: done; verdict: complete the missing step first Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for every secondhand purchase, and use it strictly for electronics, furniture, and anything with moving parts or hidden wear. Do not pay before inspection for any reason, including a claim that another buyer is waiting, because that claim is pressure, not information. Do not accept an item whose serial marks have been removed or obscured without understanding why. Do not use this record as a professional appraisal, because inspection by a buyer is a check, not a valuation. title: Pay Inside the Platform
body:
Paying inside the platform is the secondhand buyer's strongest protection, because the platform's payment channel carries the record, the identity trail, and the dispute route that a private transfer deliberately avoids. When payment moves inside the platform, the transaction is tied to the listing, the messages, and the seller's account, so a failure can be investigated from evidence. When payment moves outside at the seller's request, all three are surrendered at once, which is why every off-platform payment request should be treated as the fraud's mechanism rather than as a convenience, a discount, or a favor.

Method. The working method for this record is a payment-channel rule applied without exception. First, identify the platform's own payment channel before discussing price. Second, pay only through that channel, and keep the conversation on the platform as well, because the conversation is part of the evidence. Third, if the seller requests an outside payment method, refuse and keep the request in the message record. Fourth, if the seller insists, abandon the deal and report the account through the platform. Fifth, the demo applies the rule to four example payment proposals and prints the verdict for each.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for pay inside the platform. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: platform payment -> ACCEPT; bank transfer requested by seller -> REFUSE; gift cards requested by seller -> REFUSE and report; cash on collection with inspection -> ACCEPT with inspection and receipt; rule: the platform channel carries the record, the identity trail, and the dispute route Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for every marketplace purchase, and use it as a household rule that no discount overrides, because the discount for paying outside is paid for with protection. Do not accept a story about platform fees or account problems as a reason to pay outside, because the story is the script. Do not use this record as legal advice about any particular platform's terms, which govern that platform's transactions. Do not confuse paying inside the platform with paying safely in every respect, because inspection and seller checks still apply. title: Read Seller History Honestly
body:
Reading seller history honestly means looking for the shape of a real trading life rather than a single flattering number, because feedback scores can be inflated, accounts can be fresh, and a long history in one kind of goods says little about another. An honest history shows sales spread over months, feedback from different buyers, a mix of item types, and responses to problems that read as human rather than defensive. A dishonest or thin history shows the opposite: a new account with a burst of praise, feedback only from a few accounts, identical wording across reviews, or a gap where the account went silent and returned under pressure.

Method. The working method for this record is a history-shape check over four signals. First, check the account's age and whether sales spread over months rather than days. Second, check whether feedback comes from varied buyers rather than a few repeated accounts. Third, check whether the wording of feedback is varied and specific rather than repeated and generic. Fourth, check how the seller handled a problem, because a seller who fixed a problem in public is more trustworthy than a seller with no problems at all. Fifth, combine the signals: three or four genuine signals mean proceed with normal checks, fewer mean demand stronger inspection and platform payment, or walk away. The demo scores an example seller history on the four signals.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for read seller history honestly. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: genuine history signals: 2 of 4; sales spread over months: NO; feedback from varied buyers: yes; varied specific wording: yes; problems handled openly: NO; verdict: demand inspection and platform payment, or walk away Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for every marketplace seller, and use it hardest for high-value items and sellers with few sales. Do not treat a perfect score as proof of honesty, because histories can be manufactured, which is why inspection and platform payment still apply. Do not punish a new seller merely for being new; instead, require the protections that make a new seller safe to try. Do not use this record to accuse any individual seller, because it judges patterns, not people. title: Photograph Everything Before Handover
body:
Photographing everything before handover is the cheapest insurance in secondhand trading, because a dispute after handover is decided by what can be shown, and memory is the weakest exhibit. The buyer photographs the item's condition, its identifying marks, the accessories included, and the seller's listing alongside the item where possible, and the seller photographs the item's condition at handover too, because the same photographs protect both sides. Taken before money moves, these photographs fix the item's state at the moment of transfer; taken afterward, they prove only that a photograph was taken.

Method. The working method for this record is a handover photograph checklist. First, list the photographs to take: overall condition, close views of wear or damage, identifying marks, included accessories, and the item with its listing or agreed description. Second, take each photograph before payment and handover, with the date visible in the device's own record. Third, share the set with the other party or keep it with the transaction record. Fourth, if damage is found in the photographs that the listing did not disclose, renegotiate or walk away before paying. Fifth, the demo checks an example photograph set of five shots with one missing and names the missing shot.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for photograph everything before handover. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: handover photographs taken: 4 of 5; overall condition: taken; wear and damage close-ups: taken; identifying marks: MISSING; included accessories: taken; item with listing: taken; verdict: take the missing shot before paying Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for every secondhand handover, and use it strictly for high-value items, electronics, and anything where condition is the deal. Do not photograph another person's private property beyond the item being sold, and do not use photographs to embarrass or threaten the other party. Do not rely on the platform's listing photographs alone, because listings change and handover condition is what matters. Do not use this record as legal advice about evidence, which is governed by the applicable dispute route's own rules. title: Test Electronics on the Spot
body:
Testing electronics on the spot is the difference between buying a working device and buying a story about one, because electronics fail in ways photographs cannot show: a battery that dies in minutes, a screen with dead zones, a port that charges only at one angle, a speaker that crackles at volume, and software locks that appear only after sign-in. The test is short and should be agreed before meeting: power on, screen and touch or keys, sound, ports and charging, camera where fitted, and any account lock or activation screen. A seller who will not allow this test is not protecting the device; they are protecting the sale.

Method. The working method for this record is a spot-test checklist run before payment. First, list the tests for the device type: power and battery behavior, display and input, sound, connectivity and charging, and account or activation status. Second, run each test in front of the seller, taking the time it needs. Third, mark each test pass or fail and read the verdict: all passed mean pay as agreed, one failed mean renegotiate or walk away, and an activation lock present means do not buy at all until the lock is removed by the seller in front of you. Fourth, record the test results with the handover photographs. Fifth, the demo runs the checklist on an example device passing four of five tests and names the failure.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for test electronics on the spot. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: spot tests passed: 4 of 5; powers on and holds charge briefly: pass; display and input work: pass; sound clear: FAIL; charging and ports work: pass; no account or activation lock: pass; verdict: renegotiate or walk away Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for every secondhand electronic device, including phones, laptops, consoles, and audio gear. Do not buy a device that is still signed into the previous owner's account or locked to it, because such a device may become unusable and its history is not yours to inherit. Do not accept a test performed only by the seller's hands; the buyer should operate the device. Do not use this record as a professional diagnostic, because spot testing finds common faults, not every fault. title: Price Sense: Too Good to Be True
body:
Price sense in secondhand buying is the discipline of comparing an asking price with the range other sellers ask for the same item in similar condition, because a price far below that range is information, not luck. Genuine reasons for a low price exist: a quick sale, cosmetic damage honestly disclosed, or missing accessories. But a price far below the range with no disclosed reason describes one of three things: a fake, a faulty item, or a lure for an advance-fee or off-platform fraud. The buyer's job is to ask which one, and to require the answer to be shown in the item rather than told in a story.

Method. The working method for this record is a price-sense comparison. First, gather three or more comparable listings for the same item in similar condition and note their prices as worked-example inputs. Second, compute the typical price as the middle value of the comparables. Third, compute the asking price's distance below the typical price as a percentage. Fourth, read the verdict: within a modest distance means plausible, a large distance with a disclosed reason means inspect harder, and a large distance with no reason means treat the listing as a lure until inspection proves otherwise. Fifth, the demo compares an example asking price with three comparables and prints the distance and verdict.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for price sense: too good to be true. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: comparable prices: [120.0, 135.0, 150.0]; typical price: 135.00; asking price: 60.00; below typical by: 55.6%; verdict: treat as a lure until inspection proves otherwise Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for every secondhand purchase where the price is the main attraction, and use it strictly for branded and high-value goods. Do not use a low price alone as proof of fraud, because genuine bargains exist and insulting a genuine seller loses a good deal. Do not use a typical price computed from too few or incomparable listings; condition, accessories, and age must match. Do not let price sense override inspection, because even a fairly priced item can be faulty. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

title: Counterfeit Checks for Branded Goods
body:
Counterfeit checks for branded secondhand goods protect the buyer twice: against paying a genuine price for a fake, and against owning an item whose safety testing and warranty do not exist. The checks compare the item with the manufacturer's own information rather than with the seller's assurances: markings and fonts, stitching and materials, serial or code placement, packaging and documentation, and the price against authorized sellers. No single check proves genuineness, because good fakes copy single features well; the verdict comes from the pattern, and a pattern with several failures is a refusal even when the item looks convincing.

Method. The working method for this record is an authentication pattern score. First, list the checks: markings match the manufacturer's information, materials and finish match, serial or code present and plausible, packaging and documentation consistent, and price gap explained. Second, examine the item against each check. Third, read the verdict: four or five passes mean proceed with normal checks, three mean seek an expert opinion before paying, and fewer mean do not buy. Fourth, keep the examination photographs with the transaction record. Fifth, the demo scores an example branded item passing three checks and prints the seek-expert-opinion verdict.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for counterfeit checks for branded goods. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: authentication checks passed: 3 of 5; markings match manufacturer info: pass; materials and finish match: FAIL; serial or code plausible: pass; packaging and documents consistent: pass; price gap explained: FAIL; verdict: seek an expert opinion first Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for branded goods, safety-critical goods, and any item where the brand carries the value or the safety. Do not use a convincing logo alone as proof, because logos are the easiest feature to copy. Do not buy safety-critical counterfeits at any price, because the failure mode is injury rather than disappointment. Do not use this record as an expert authentication, because expert authentication is a separate service with its own methods. title: Vehicles and High-Value Items: Extra Steps
body:
Vehicles and high-value items deserve extra steps because their prices justify more fraud and their faults cost more to discover, and the ordinary secondhand routine, while necessary, is not sufficient for them. The extra steps are documentary rather than merely visual: the item's history and ownership records where such records exist, an independent inspection by a qualified person, verification that identifying numbers match the documents, and payment through a channel that leaves a complete record. A seller who resists documentary checks for a high-value item is not being private; they are asking the buyer to carry a risk the documents would have carried.

Method. The working method for this record is an extra-steps checklist for high-value secondhand purchases. First, list the steps: ownership and history records checked, identifying numbers matched to documents, independent inspection completed, payment channel recorded, and written agreement of price and condition. Second, mark each step done or missing. Third, read the verdict: all steps done mean proceed, one missing means complete it before paying, and more missing mean do not pay yet. Fourth, keep the documents with the transaction record. Fifth, the demo scores an example high-value purchase completing four of five steps and names the missing step.

Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Do not skip the independent inspection for a vehicle or a complex machine, because a buyer's eye cannot see internal wear. Do not accept documents that do not match the item's identifying numbers. title: Shipping Secondhand Safely
body:
Shipping secondhand goods safely is a shared responsibility that must be agreed before the parcel moves, because after dispatch the buyer cannot inspect and the seller cannot re-pack, and every ambiguity becomes a dispute. The agreement covers who pays the shipping cost, which service and tracking level is used, how the item is packed and photographed before dispatch, what happens if the item arrives damaged, and who bears the return cost if the item is not as described. Written in the platform's messages, this agreement is evidence; left verbal or vague, it is a misunderstanding waiting for a damaged parcel to reveal it.

Method. The working method for this record is a shipping agreement check with cost arithmetic. title: Returns Between Private Sellers
body:
Returns between private sellers work differently from retail returns, and expecting retail rules in a private sale is the misunderstanding that creates most secondhand disputes. A private seller generally sells as seen and described, which means the buyer's protection comes from accurate description, inspection before payment, and the platform's own rules, rather than from a general right to change one's mind. The practical rule is therefore agreed before payment: what happens if the item is not as described, how quickly the buyer must report it, who pays return shipping, and what evidence is required. Agreed in writing, these terms are fair to both sides; assumed silently, they are a dispute.

Method. The working method for this record is a return-terms agreement check. First, list the terms to agree: accuracy standard, reporting deadline, return shipping payer, refund timing, and evidence required. Second, mark each term agreed or open. Third, read the verdict: all terms agreed mean the deal can proceed on understood terms, any open term means agree it in writing before paying. Fourth, after delivery, report any not-as-described problem within the agreed deadline with photographs, because late reports lose credibility even when they are true. Fifth, the demo checks an example return agreement with all terms agreed and prints the proceed verdict.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for returns between private sellers. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: return terms agreed: 5 of 5; open terms: []; verdict: proceed on understood terms Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for every secondhand purchase, and use it strictly for items bought without inspection, such as shipped goods. Do not assume a right to return for change of mind in a private sale unless the seller or platform grants it. Do not delay reporting a genuine problem, because deadlines run from delivery, not from convenience. Do not use this record as legal advice about consumer rights in private sales, which vary by jurisdiction and by platform, and are governed by the applicable law and the platform's own terms. title: Scam Scripts: Advance Fees and Fake Couriers
body:
Advance-fee and fake-courier scripts are the secondhand market's most expensive fictions, because they charge the buyer for a delivery that never happens and then charge again for its release. The advance-fee version asks for a deposit, a reservation fee, or a shipping payment before the item is seen, often for an item priced to tempt. The fake-courier version follows with a message claiming the parcel is held and needs a fee, a tax, or an insurance payment to move, with a link that harvests payment details. Both scripts share one tell: money is demanded before the item, the inspection, or the platform's protection has any part in the deal.

Method. The working method for this record is scam-script recognition over the conversation. First, list the script markers: payment before inspection, fee to release a held parcel, link from an unexpected message, pressure to act immediately, and refusal to meet or use the platform channel. Second, mark each marker present or absent in the conversation. Third, read the verdict: zero markers mean proceed with normal checks, one marker means stop and verify through the platform independently, and two or more mean stop, keep the conversation as evidence, and report the account. Fourth, never pay a release fee from a message link; verify delivery only through the platform or carrier's own site. Fifth, the demo scores an example conversation showing three markers and prints the stop-and-report verdict.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for scam scripts: advance fees and fake couriers. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: script markers found: 3; - payment before inspection; - fee to release held parcel; - link from unexpected message; verdict: stop, keep the conversation, report the account Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for every secondhand conversation, and teach it as a household rule, because these scripts target politeness, haste, and desire. Do not pay any fee to release a parcel that you did not agree to in the platform's own messages. Do not follow delivery links from unexpected messages. Do not argue with a scripted account; stopping and reporting is the complete response. Do not use this record to accuse a legitimate seller whose genuine delivery problem looks similar; the verdict concerns the pattern, and independent verification through the platform resolves the doubt. title: Stolen-Goods Red Flags and What to Do
body:
Stolen-goods red flags matter because buying a stolen item harms its true owner, risks confiscation without refund, and can draw the buyer into a police matter, all for a bargain that was never a bargain. The flags are practical rather than legalistic: a price far below comparable items with no reason, identifying marks removed or obscured, a seller who cannot explain where the item came from, pressure to complete quickly and quietly, and an item type that is frequently stolen offered in unusual quantity. Any one flag may be innocent, but several together describe an item whose history the seller does not want examined, and that is the point at which a careful buyer walks away.

Method. The working method for this record is a red-flag count with a defined response. First, list the flags: unexplained low price, removed or obscured marks, vague or shifting origin story, pressure for speed and silence, and unusual quantity of a commonly stolen type. Second, mark each flag present or absent. Third, read the verdict: zero or one flag means proceed with normal checks, two flags mean demand a clear origin account and documentary proof before proceeding, and three or more mean walk away and consider reporting the listing to the platform. Fourth, if an item already bought proves stolen, the buyer should seek advice from the platform and the relevant authorities rather than reselling it, because passing it on repeats the harm. Fifth, the demo scores an example listing showing two flags and prints the demand-proof verdict.

Do not buy an item whose identifying marks have been deliberately removed, because removal has no innocent purpose in a sale. title: Children's Items and Safety Recalls
body:
Children's secondhand items carry safety rules that other goods do not, because a child's item can be recalled, damaged invisibly, or missing a safety part while still looking perfectly usable. The buyer's check is therefore documentary as well as visual: identify the item's make, model, and production markings, check the official recall listings of the relevant authority for that item, inspect for missing safety parts, broken mechanisms, and recalled components, and refuse any item whose safety status cannot be established. A bargain on a child's item is not a bargain when its safety is unknown, because the cost of being wrong is paid by a child.

Method. The working method for this record is a children's-item safety check. First, record the item's identifying details: make, model, and markings. Second, check the relevant authority's official recall listings for those details, and record the result. Third, inspect for missing safety parts, damage, and wear that affects safety. Fourth, read the verdict: no recall found and inspection passed mean proceed with normal checks, any recall found means do not buy, and unknown safety status means do not buy until the status is established. Fifth, the demo runs the check on an example item with no recall found and inspection passed, and prints the proceed verdict with the rule that an unknown status is a refusal.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for children's items and safety recalls. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Do not buy a child's item with missing safety parts, broken mechanisms, or an unknown recall status. Do not rely on the seller's assurance about recalls; check the official listings yourself. title: Refurbished vs Used vs Reconditioned
body:
Refurbished, used, and reconditioned are three different promises that sellers often use as if they were one word, and the buyer's protection depends on knowing which promise was actually made. Used means sold as it is, with wear and history, and the buyer's check is inspection. Refurbished typically means inspected, repaired where needed, cleaned, and tested, often with a stated warranty from the refurbisher. Reconditioned sits between these in common usage, usually meaning restored to working order without the full refurbishment process, but its meaning varies by seller, which is why the word alone should never be trusted: the written description of what was done, what was replaced, and what warranty applies is the promise, and the label is only its nickname.

Method. The working method for this record is condition-grade classification from the seller's written description. First, read the description for the three facts that define the grade: what inspection was done, what parts were replaced or repaired, and what warranty applies and from whom. Second, classify the offer: all three facts stated with a refurbisher warranty mean refurbished, wear disclosed without repair claims mean used, and partial repair claims without a full warranty mean reconditioned or unclear. Third, if the label and the facts disagree, trust the facts and treat the label as marketing. Fourth, price the offer against the same grade elsewhere, not against a better grade. Fifth, the demo classifies three example descriptions and prints each grade.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for refurbished vs used vs reconditioned. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: refurbished: inspected, battery replaced, 12-month refurbisher warranty; used: wear disclosed, sold as seen, no warranty; reconditioned or unclear: cleaned and tested, no parts replaced, 30-day seller warranty; rule: trust the written facts, not the label alone Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for every secondhand purchase where the condition word affects the price, and use it strictly for electronics and appliances where refurbishment claims are common. Do not pay a refurbished price for a used description, because the price gap is the value of the work and warranty claimed. Do not accept a refurbishment claim without the written facts behind it. Do not use this record as a legal definition of these terms, which are not uniformly defined by law and vary by seller and platform. title: Build a Secondhand Buying Routine
body:
A secondhand buying routine turns separate cautions into one habit that runs before, during, and after every purchase, because desire and urgency defeat memory and routines do not. The routine has three phases: before meeting, read the seller's history and the listing as evidence and agree the meeting place; during the exchange, inspect, test, photograph, and pay inside the platform; after handover, check the item fully within the agreed window and keep the record. Written down and consulted before each purchase, the routine is a practice rather than a principle, and after any bad experience it is reviewed, because a routine that failed once contains the lesson for its own repair.

Method. The working method for this record is a routine checklist scored across the three phases. First, list the routine's steps: seller history read, safe meeting agreed, inspection and testing done, handover photographed, platform payment used, and record kept. Second, mark each step done or missed for a recent purchase. Third, score the routine: all six done mean the routine held, four or five mean name the missed step and fix it next time, and fewer mean the routine is not yet a routine and must be written down and consulted before the next purchase. Fourth, the missed steps are printed by name. Fifth, the demo scores an example purchase following five of six steps and names the missed step.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for build a secondhand buying routine. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: routine steps followed: 5 of 6; missed: ['handover photographed']; routine verdict: fix the missed step next time Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record as the household's secondhand rule, taught to everyone who buys or sells, because the routine protects the whole household's money and safety. Do not treat the routine as a guarantee, because no routine defeats every fraud, which is why platform payment and prompt reporting remain the backstops. Do not let the routine grow so long that it is skipped; six steps followed always beat twenty steps followed sometimes. Do not use this record as legal advice, because rights and remedies vary by platform and jurisdiction.
